extracted.intended_audience: early career researchers (peer reviewers and authors)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide for early career researchers on how peer review works and how to perform high-quality reviews for journals and grant bodies, including ethics, types of review, and how editors select work and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge validity, significance and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review judges the validity, significance and originality of the work, rather than the person who has done it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the research methods, data and conclusions are valid and significant; this is the core purpose of peer review as a 'quality mark' for research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and fit to journal (desk review criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors screen submissions for relevance to the journal, fit with scope, format and length, clarity of discussion, research methods and overall fit with the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an initial quick 'desk review' (around two weeks) that filters many papers before full peer review; being 'groundbreaking' or suitable for the journal's audience matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the study innovative or original? Does the work challenge existing paradigms or add to existing knowledge?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the research question is novel and whether the paper meaningfully advances the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance / significance of the question
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it matter? Are the questions addressed important?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the broader importance and potential impact of the findings when recommending publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of research question
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the research question clear?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear, well-defined question is essential for judging whether the methods and analyses appropriately address it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of approach and study design
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the approach appropriate? Are the study design, methods and analysis appropriate to the question being studied?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chosen methods can validly answer the research question and whether experimental design decisions (controls, randomisation, blinding) are adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and adequacy of methods description (replicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the methods described clearly enough for other researchers to replicate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess completeness and transparency of methods and whether additional details or protocols are needed for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis and treatment of uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the statistical analyses and level of uncertainty in the data treated appropriately?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack statistical expertise, state this and recommend a specialised statistical review; many journals now employ statistical reviewers to supplement subject reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of data and reliability of conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the quality of the data and whether the conclusions are reliable and supported by the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for underpowered studies, inappropriate analyses, overinterpretation of results, and whether conclusions match the evidence presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of results and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the presentation of the results be improved and do they answer the question?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer suggestions for clearer figures, tables, or text to make the results and their implications more understandable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the discussion take into account the limitations of the study?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reviews should check that authors acknowledge limitations and avoid overstating findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the conclusions appropriate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that conclusions follow logically from the analyses and do not extend beyond what the data support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics approvals and ethical conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If humans, human tissues or animals are involved, was ethics approval gained and was the study ethical?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag missing or inadequate ethical approvals to the editor; consider consent, welfare and relevant regulatory compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare any conflicts of interest to the editor and be transparent about collaborations or close relationships with authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts need not automatically preclude reviewing but must be disclosed so editors can judge suitability; suggest alternative reviewers if unable to be impartial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and permission for co-reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be carried out in confidence; if a colleague or supervisor participates in a review, let the editor know so work can be credited appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not share manuscripts without editor permission; when co-reviewing, ensure the editor approves and acknowledge contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and commitment to deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Only accept review invitations if you can submit within the requested time frame; if you cannot complete the review, inform the journal promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors track reviewer speed and may avoid inviting frequently slow reviewers; prompt communication preserves goodwill and reduces author frustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional, constructive tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a fair, robust and timely critique that is useful for authors; be professional and constructive in your approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember you're an author too; avoid personal attacks, leave time (e.g., 24 hours) between reading and writing to temper nitpicking, and aim to help authors improve the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of expertise and honesty about limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor will not expect you to comment beyond your areas of expertise; provide subject-specific comments and flag aspects (e.g., statistics) that need specialist review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack confidence in an area, recommend additional reviewers or a statistical expert, and explicitly state limits in your report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reporting guidelines and structured review forms
rubrics_metrics.description: What is expected varies by journal; many will ask you to answer specific questions or use reporting guidelines during review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the journal's online form and any recommended reporting checklists (e.g., CONSORT, PRISMA) and contact the editorial office if unsure what to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting plagiarism and fraud (limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should notify the editor if they suspect plagiarism; peer review can catch some plagiarism and fraud but cannot be relied upon to detect all instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journals use plagiarism-checking software and editors may consult reviewers about flagged similarities; fabricated data can be very hard to detect unless it contains obvious anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recognition and reward expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers desire recognition; journals may provide certificates, accreditation (CME/CPD), acknowledgements, or platforms (Publons, ORCiD) to record reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of available recognition routes; opinions vary on direct payment due to potential bias concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: How editors use reviewer input to decide
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors combine reviewers' opinions with editorial judgement, considering reviewers' expertise, specific scientific points, feasibility of requested revisions, and overall conceptual interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should provide clear, evidence-based comments and recommendations noting the strength and relevance of their expertise to guide editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for reviewers (visibility and credentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be selected as a reviewer, be visible: maintain an academic profile with contact info and expertise; volunteer to journals and co-review with supervisors if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors find reviewers via personal knowledge, PubMed searches, and bibliographies; early career researchers can be invited to co-review or directly volunteer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding review models and their trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Different peer review types (single-blind, double-blind, open) have distinct pros and cons relating to bias, accountability, transparency and potential repercussions for reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-blind: common, allows honest reviews but can enable abuse; double-blind: reduces some bias but anonymisation is imperfect; open review: increases accountability and transparency but may deter reviewers and risk reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferable (cascading) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferable peer review is when previous reviewers' reports for a rejected paper are reused when submitted to another journal to reduce review wastage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may reserve the right to invite new reviews; services like Review Commons offer journal-independent reviews that authors can use across journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered reports (peer review before results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered reports are peer-reviewed at the stage of methods and analyses before data collection; journals provisionally accept studies that pass this review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach evaluates scientific reasoning and methods beforehand and helps avoid publication bias against null or negative results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can extend beyond publication through post-publication review, publication of reviewer reports, author replies and editorial correspondence to increase transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals publish reviewer reports alongside papers and allow rapid responses or letters, enabling ongoing scrutiny and improving trust in the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Becoming a better reviewer (training and mentorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn to review through mentorship from experienced reviewers, training days, online courses, and resources from publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available resources (Elsevier Researcher Academy, Publons Academy, PLOS Reviewer Centre, Nature Masterclasses, Wiley, Sage) and consider asking to co-review with an experienced mentor.
